docs.title: Command Mode
docs.text:
Similar to the previous versions of the BlueSMiRF, all communication with the device is retransmitted between its Bluetooth serial link and UART interface. To configure the device, you must send a command key within the first 60 seconds after power-on or reset. This will trigger the device to pause the datastream and enter command mode, where the device settings can be configured using a set of AT-commands.

Command Key

  • UART Interface: $$$
  • Bluetooth Serial Link: +++ (remote access)

Tip

The settings of the command key can be reconfigured with the following commands:

  • AT-BluetoothEscapeCharacter
  • AT-EscapeCharacter
  • AT-EscapeCharacterCount
  • AT-MaxCommandTimeMs
    • By default, the command key can only be sent during the first 60 seconds after powering or resetting the device.

Once the BlueSMiRF v2 recognizes the command key, it responds with OK; and the CONNECT and STATUS LEDs will blink together. AT-commands must be sent one at a time, each ending with a carriage return (Enter). The device will echo the AT-command and return OK on success, or ERROR if the input is invalid.

Response acknowledging user is in command mode.

Note

Depending on your serial terminal's settings, you may not see the characters that are being sent. You can try turning on the local echo to view the characters. However, keep in mind that any characters sent when the BlueSMiRF v2 is in command mode will already be echoed back.

docs.title: AT-Commands
docs.text:
Below is a full list of the available AT-commands. The AT-commands and parameter names are not case sensitive, but parameter values are. This distinction is important when configuring the device settings, such as the WiFi SSID and password.

AT Command Command Description $$$ Enter Command Mode - Hardware connection +++ Enter Command Mode - Bluetooth connection AT Reports OK AT? Display this help text ATA Display all settings ATB Display Bluetooth settings ATC Check for new firmware ATD Display the debug settings ATF Restore factory settings ATM Display MAC address ATP Start pairing process ATS Display serial settings ATU Update Firmware ATV Display firmware version ATW Save current settings to NVM ATX Exit command mode ATY Display system settings ATZ Reboot the system AT-<Param>=<value> Set parameter's value to xxx by name (Param) AT-<Param> Print parameter's current value by name (Param)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
The parameters <Param> are used to query and configure specific device settings. Sending the AT-<Param> AT-command without a value, will querry the device setting and respond with the current value followed by an OK. Meanwhile, a parameter's value is configured by sending AT-<Param>=<value> AT-command. Use the ATW AT-command to store the new value in NVM (non-volatile memory).

Example

AT-BluetoothNickname=MyBlueSMiRF
AT-BluetoothNickname
ATW
ATX

The first command sets the Bluetooth broadcast name, the second reads it back, ATW saves the changed settings to non-volatile memory (NVM), and ATX exits command mode.

These parameters are best discussed in groups:

  • Bluetooth Parameters
  • Serial Parameters
  • System Parameters

docs.title: Bluetooth Parameters
docs.text:
Below is a table of AT-commands used to query or configure the Bluetooth parameters, a short description of the commands, and its factory default value (if applicable). Right after the table, there is also a list which provides a detailed explanation of each parameters' effect on the device settings.

AT Command Command Description Factory Default Value AT-BluetoothConnectRetries Number of retries of a paired connection 5 AT-BluetoothConnectTimeoutMs Milliseconds before a paired connection attempt times out 3000 AT-BluetoothEscapeCharacter The character received from the remote system, sought to enter command mode + AT-BluetoothNickname User configurable name to broadcast over Bluetooth during discovery BlueSMiRF-ABCD, where ABCD is the last four digits of the MAC address AT-BluetoothPairedMac MAC address of the unit that the user wants to connect to at startup AT-BluetoothPairedName Name of the unit that the user wants to connect to at startup AT-BluetoothPin Pin to enter during pairing - only required for older Bluetooth devices 1234 AT-BluetoothRxSize Bluetooth receive buffer size 2048 AT-BluetoothTxSize Bluetooth write buffer size 1024 AT-BluetoothType Bluetooth protocol used for communication 0
  • BluetoothConnectRetries If this device has a paired MAC or name, at power up it will attempt to connect to this paired device. A connection is not guaranteed, and the connection will be re-tried this number of times before going into passive, discoverable mode.
  • BluetoothConnectTimeoutMs When this device is connecting to a paired device, if this number of milliseconds expires before a connection is made, the device will attempt to reconnect to the paired device.
  • BluetoothEscapeCharacter This is the character that must be transmitted by a remote device to enter command mode remotely over the Bluetooth connection.

    Note

    Escape characters are ignored after MaxCommandTimeMs number of milliseconds and within MinEscapeTimeMs of other incoming characters.

  • BluetoothNickname The name that is broadcast when other devices are scanning for devices to pair to.
  • BluetoothPairedMac The MAC address of the BlueSMiRF that this device should pair to at power-on. Use the ATM command on the remote device to display its MAC address. This command is not normally used; use the button pairing method for an easier way to pair two devices.
  • BluetoothPairedName The name of the BlueSMiRF that this device should pair to at power-on. Use the BluetoothNickname command on the remote device to change its paired name. This command is not normally used; use the button pairing method for an easier way to pair two devices.
  • BluetoothPin The pin that is needed during pairing. Only needed on very old Bluetooth USB dongles.
  • BluetoothRxSize The size of the Bluetooth receive buffer. Increase if a large amount of data is coming into the BlueSMiRF over Bluetooth, before the speed of the serial interface can output it.
  • BluetoothTxSize The size of the Bluetooth transmit buffer. Increase if a large amount of data needs to be transmitted over Bluetooth but the connection between devices is poor and multiple retransmissions occur.
  • BluetoothType Controls the Bluetooth protocol. This parameter accepts a 0, 1, and 2 for the Bluetooth Protocol as listed below. Note that only the SPP protocol supports pairing.
    • Protocol 0 = Serial Port Profile (SPP)
    • Protocol 1 = Bluetooth Low-Energy (BLE)
    • Protocol 2 = Radio off

docs.title: Serial Parameters
docs.text:
Below is a table of AT-commands used to query or configure the serial parameters, a short description of the commands, and its factory default value (if applicable). Right after the table, there is also a list which provides a detailed explanation of each parameters' effect on the device settings.

AT Command Command Description Factory Default Value AT-FlowControl Enable the use of CTS/RTS flow control signals 0 AT-InvertCts Invert the input of CTS 0 AT-InvertRts Invert the output of RTS 0 AT-PartialFrameTimeoutMs Send partial buffer if time expires 50 AT-RtsStartSendingPercent Percent of serialReceiveBuffer that is free when RTS is asserted 25 AT-RtsStopSendingPercent Percent of serialReceiveBuffer that is free when RTS is deasserted 5 AT-SerialReceiveBufferSize Serial receive buffer size 51200 AT-SerialSpeed The baud rate that the BlueSMiRF operates at. 115200 AT-SerialTransmitBufferSize Buffer size to receive bytes from Bluetooth 10240
  • FlowControl If flow control is enabled, the BlueSMiRF v2 will send data when its CTS pin is driven low (the host system is telling the radio to transmit). If flow control is enabled, BlueSMiRF v2 will drive its RTS low if its serial buffer is full (the radio is telling the host system to hold its horses). By default, flow control is turned off.
  • InvertCts By default, InvertCts is false and CTS is high when data is allowed to flow. Enable InvertCts to do the opposite.
  • InvertRts By default, InvertRts is false and RTS is high when data is allowed to flow. Enable InvertRts to do the opposite.
  • PartialFrameTimeoutMs The number of milliseconds of timeout before a partial packet is sent. For example, if a partial frame of 12 bytes is received, the radio will wait this amount for more bytes before initiating a transmission.
  • RtsStartSendingPercent Percent of serialReceiveBuffer that is free when RTS is asserted. Default of 25% of serialReceiveBuffer.
  • RtsStopSendingPercent Percent of serialReceiveBuffer that is free when RTS is deasserted. Default of 5% of serialReceiveBuffer.
  • SerialReceiveBufferSize Buffer size to receive serial data from the serial port, to be sent over Bluetooth. The default is 51200.
  • SerialSpeed The baud rate that the BlueSMiRF operates at. Discrete values 2400, 4800, 9600, 14400, 19200, 38400, 57600, 115200 (default), 230400, 460800, and 921600bps are allowed.
  • SerialTransmitBufferSize Buffer size to receive bytes from Bluetooth, waiting to be printed out the UART. The default is 10240.

docs.title: System Parameters
docs.text:
Below is a table of AT-commands used to query or configure the system parameters, a short description of the commands, and its factory default value (if applicable). Right after the table, there is also a list which provides a detailed explanation of each parameters' effect on the device settings.

AT Command Command Description Factory Default Value AT-EscapeCharacter The character sought to enter command mode $ AT-EscapeCharacterCount The number of escape characters required to enter command mode 3 AT-LedStyle Controls the behavior of the Status and Connect LEDs 0 AT-MaxCommandTimeMs After this time in milliseconds, command mode cannot be entered 60000 AT-MinEscapeTimeMs Serial traffic must stop this amount of milliseconds before an escape character is recognized 2000 AT-PSRAMThreshold Use PSRAM for memory requests larger than this number of bytes 1000 AT-WiFiPassword Password for the SSID, used for over-the-air-updates AT-WiFiSSID SSID used for over-the-air-updates

Warning

The ESP32 Pico-Mini is only compatible with 2.4GHz WiFi networks; it will not work on the 5GHz bands.

  • EscapeCharacter The character that must be entered a number of times (EscapeCharacterCount) to enter configuration mode. An escape character must be entered before the max time of MaxCommandTimeMs and after MinEscapeTimeMs.
  • EscapeCharacterCount The number of escape characters needed before command mode is entered. Set to 0 to disable.
  • LedStyle Modes of how the LEDs behave:
    • 0 - CLASSIC (default): The STATUS LED blinks with TX/RX traffic.
    • 1 - SERIAL_TRAFFIC: The CONNECT LED blinks with TX traffic and the STATUS LED blinks with RX traffic.
    • 2 - OFF: The CONNECT and STATUS LEDs are turned off.
  • MaxCommandTimeMs Once this number of milliseconds has passed, command mode cannot be entered. This is used as a method to prevent a remote system from accidentally entering command mode.
  • MinEscapeTimeMs This number of milliseconds must pass between the last serial character received and an escape character. This is used as a method to prevent a remote system from accidentally entering command mode.
  • AT-PSRAMThreshold The memory threshold, before PSRAM is enabled
  • WiFiPassword The password for the local WiFi; used for firmware updates.
  • WiFiSSID The SSID for the local WiFi; used for firmware updates.

    The ESP32 Pico-Mini is only compatible with 2.4GHz WiFi networks; it will not work on the 5GHz bands

docs.title: Button Operation
docs.text:
The PAIR button on the BlueSMiRF v2 allows the device to enter a few different states.

  • Pairing Mode
  • Discoverable Mode
  • Factory Reset Mode
  • Bootloader Mode

docs.title: Serial Link
docs.text:
In its default configuration, users can simply scan for and connect to the BlueSMiRF v2, from their phone or a laptop using a Bluetooth connection. However, for a serial bridge between two BlueSMiRF v2 boards, one board needs to be in discoverable mode, before the other device enters pairing mode and creates its connection.

  1. Device 1: Hold its PAIR button held for 4 to 8 seconds then released.
  2. Device 1: Enters pairing mode and will scan for any devices in discoverable mode.
  3. Device 1: When Device 1 fails to discover any available devices, it will enter discoverable mode and become available for pairing.
    • Device 1 will broadcast the name BlueSMiRF-Pairing and wait for an incoming connection.
  4. Device 2: Hold its PAIR button held for 4 to 8 seconds, then released.
  5. Device 2: Will then enter pairing mode and scan for any compatible devices to pair with.
    • The scan should find that Device 1 is in discoverable mode broadcasting the BlueSMiRF-Pairing name.
  6. Device 2: Connects to Device 1
    • Device 2 stores the MAC address of Device 1
    • Whenever Device 2 boots up, it will always try to connect to the stored the MAC address (i.e. Device 1).
  7. Device 1: Remains agnostic of any connections or pairing; no MAC address has been stored on it.
    • When Device 1 boots, it will not attempt to connect to any devices.

docs.title: Pairing Mode
docs.text:
Pairing mode is used to scan and connect to other BlueSMiRF v2 devices in discoverable mode.

GIF Setting BlueSMiRF v2 in Pairing Mode

To enter pairing mode:

  1. Hold the PAIR button down
  2. Wait (~4-8 seconds) until the Status and Connect LEDs to slowly blink back and forth
  3. Release the PAIR button

Once a BlueSMiRF has entered Pairing Mode, it will scan for other compatible BlueSMiRF devices.

If a second device enters Pairing Mode, it will scan for other compatible BlueSMiRF devices broadcasting the name (you guessed it) 'BlueSMiRF-Pairing'. If a device is detected, the second device will connect to the first device, store the MAC address of the first device, and attempt to connect to it at every future power on. The first device will not be aware of or connect to another device at power on.

If no other compatible device is found after a few seconds, the BlueSMiRF will enter Discoverable mode.

docs.title: Discoverable Mode
docs.text:
If no other compatible device is found after a few seconds, the BlueSMiRF will enter Discoverable mode. The device will broadcast the name 'BlueSMiRF-Pairing' and wait for an incoming connection.

To enter discoverable mode:

  1. With no other devices in discoverable mode, hold the PAIR button down
  2. Wait (~4-8 seconds) until the Status and Connect LEDs to slowly blink back and forth
  3. Release the PAIR button
  4. The BlueSMiRF v2 will enter pairing mode scanned for available devices it can connect to
  5. After a few seconds, if it has failed to connect with another device, the board will enter Discoverable mode
    • In this mode, the Connect LED will slowly blink

docs.title: Factory Reset Mode
docs.text:
Holding the PAIR button for more than 8 seconds will cause the Status and Connect LEDs to quickly blink back and forth. If the PAIR button is released at this time, the device will enter Factory Reset mode.

GIF Factory Reset

After a Factory Reset, all settings are reset to default and/or erased in the following way:

  • The baud rate is set to 115200 bps.
  • The escape character is set to '$' and a count of 3.
  • The WiFi SSID and password are erased.
  • Flow control is disabled.
  • All the other system settings are returned to default.

docs.title: Bootloader Mode
docs.text:
Hold down the PAIR button when the BlueSMiRF v2 is not powered. Applying power will set the microcontroller to bootloader mode. The STATUS LED will be dim indicating that we are in Bootloader Mode. After uploading the firmware binaries to the ESP32, you will need to cycle power to the device as this does not automatically exit the bootloader mode.

GIF Setting the BlueSMiRF in Bootloader Mode

Note

As stated in the hardware assembly when connecting a USB-to-serial converter, you will need to manually wire the TX-to-RX and RX-to-TX to a USB-to-serial converter with jumper wires.

docs.title: Button Operation
docs.text:
PAIR Button on the BlueSMiRF v2.

The PAIR button on the BlueSMiRF v2 is used to enter a few different states:

  • Discoverable Mode
    • A default state, where the device is ready to be paired with a Bluetooth device.
  • BlueSMiRF Pairing Mode
    • Used to pair the BlueSMiRF v2 with another BlueSMiRF v2 in the (default) discoverable mode.
  • Bootloader Mode
    • Used to manually update the firmware through the UART interface.
  • Factory Reset
    • Forces the BlueSMiRF v2 to return to its original factory settings. Then, it returns to the (default) discoverable mode.

docs.title: Create a Serial Link
docs.text:
In its default configuration, users can simply scan for and connect to the BlueSMiRF v2, from their phone or a laptop using a Bluetooth connection. However, for a serial bridge between two BlueSMiRF v2 boards, one board needs to be in discoverable mode, before the other device enters pairing mode and creates their connection.

  1. Device 1: By default, the device be in discoverable mode and be available for pairing.
    • Device 1 will broadcast the name BlueSMiRF-Pairing and wait for an incoming connection.
  2. Device 2: Hold the PAIR button for 4 to 8 seconds, then release.
  3. Device 2: Will then enter pairing mode and scan for any compatible devices to pair with.
    • The scan should find that Device 1 is in discoverable mode broadcasting the BlueSMiRF-Pairing name.
  4. Device 2: Connects to Device 1
    • Device 2 stores the MAC address of Device 1
    • Whenever Device 2 boots up, it will always try to connect to the stored the MAC address (i.e. Device 1).
  5. Device 1: Remains agnostic of any connections or pairing; no MAC address has been stored on it.
    • When Device 1 boots, it will not attempt to connect to any devices.

Note

The BlueSMiRF that was detected (Device 1), does not store the MAC address of the pairing BlueSMiRF (Device 2). Upon restart, the BlueSMiRF (Device 1) will return to the (default) discoverable mode.

docs.title: Discoverable Mode
docs.text:
A default state, where the device will broadcast the name BlueSMiRF-Pairing, blink the Connect LED slowly, and wait for an incoming connection.

To enter discoverable mode:

  1. With no other BlueSMiRF devices in discoverable mode, hold the PAIR button down
  2. Wait (~4-8 seconds) until the Status and Connect LEDs to slowly blink back and forth
  3. Release the PAIR button
  4. The BlueSMiRF v2 will enter pairing mode and scan for available devices it can connect to
  5. After a few seconds, if it has failed to connect with another device, the board will return to its discoverable mode
    • In this mode, the Connect LED will slowly blink

Note

When the BlueSMiRF's connection is paired by another device, it does not store the MAC address of the connecting device; nor will it attempt to restore that connection upon restart.

docs.title: BlueSMiRF Pairing Mode
docs.text:
Pairing mode is used to scan and connect to other BlueSMiRF v2 devices in discoverable mode.

GIF Setting BlueSMiRF v2 in Pairing Mode

To enter pairing mode:

  1. Hold the PAIR button down
  2. Wait (~4-8 seconds) until the Status and Connect LEDs to slowly blink back and forth
  3. Release the PAIR button

Once a BlueSMiRF has entered pairing mode, it will scan for other compatible BlueSMiRF devices broadcasting the BlueSMiRF-Pairing name. If a device is detected, it will connect to the device and store the MAC address of the located device so that it can reconnect to the same device in the future. Otherwise, if no device is found after a few seconds, the BlueSMiRF will return to its discoverable mode.

docs.title: Bootloader Mode
docs.text:
Hold down the PAIR button while the BlueSMiRF v2 is not powered. Applying power will set the microcontroller to bootloader mode; the STATUS LED should also be dimmed. After uploading the firmware binaries to the ESP32, you will need to cycle power to the device, as it does not automatically hard reset.

GIF Setting the BlueSMiRF in Bootloader Mode

Tip

To automatically enable a hard reset, users can connect the DTR pin of USB-to-serial converter to the RST PTH pad of the BlueSMiRF with a IC Hook with Pigtail.

docs.title: Factory Reset
docs.text:
Holding the PAIR button for more than 8 seconds will cause the Status and Connect LEDs to quickly blink back and forth. If the PAIR button is released at this time, the device settings will be restored to their factory defaults.

GIF Factory Reset

docs.title: Device update
docs.text:
From time to time, SparkFun will release new firmware for the BlueSMiRF v2 product line to add and improve functionality. For most users, firmware can be upgraded over a 2.4GHz WiFi network using the OTA method. Users can also update the firmware manually using a Command Line Interface (CLI)

  • Arduino Board Manager URL: 
    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json

docs.title: Over-The-Air (OTA)
docs.text: Once the AT-WiFiSSID and AT-WiFiPassword settings have been entered for your local WiFi network, the ATC command can be issued to check for new firmware. If new firmware is available, send the ATU command to begin an update.

docs.title: Serial Interface
docs.text: Because it's much easier to use, we recommend the OTA firmware update process. If that fails for some reason, the following CLI method can be used.

docs.title: Bootloader Mode
docs.text:
Hold the PAIR button while powering the BlueSMiRF v2. This will cause the ESP32 to enter bootloader mode. Once the BlueSMiRF v2 is in bootloader mode, the STATUS LED will be dimly lit and the CONNECT LED will be off.

We recommend using a breadboard or jumper wires to connect the BlueSMiRF to a USB-to-Serial adapter. At a minimum, you will need to connect the UART pins, power, and ground as stated in the hardware assembly. Remember, the TX and RX connections must be crossed over.

USB-to-Serial ConverterPinout Intermediate Wire Connection BlueSMiRF v2Pinout DTR RTS RXI RXI TXO TXO 3V3 VCC CTS CTS GND GND

Note

To automatically trigger the reset of the ESP32, users can connect the DTR pin from the USB-to-Serial converter to the RST reset pin on the BlueSMiRF.

USB-to-Serial Converter (CH340) to BlueSMiRF v2 Header with an Additional Stackable Header

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Identify the COM port the USB-to-Serial device enumerated at. The easiest way to do this is to open the Device Manager under the Ports (COM & LPT) tree:

CH340 is on COM10 as shown in Device Manager

If the COM port is not showing, be sure the unit is turned On. If an unknown device is appearing, you’ll need to install drivers for your USB-to-serial device (we'll assume that you are using the CH340).

Once the correct COM port is identified, head to the GitHub repo for the BlueSMiRF v2 binaries and download all the contents. Unzip the contents in a known directory and copy the path.

Download BlueSMiRF v2 Binaries GitHub Repo (ZIP)

Open a command prompt (Win + R then type cmd). Head to the directory where you unzipped the folder. You'll need to use the cd commmand, paste the path where you unzipped the folder, and hit the Enter key.

Change Path to BlueSMiRF Binaries Folder

You'll then need to run the 'batch_program.bat' along with the binary file name and COM port. Enter the following command below, where COM4 should be replaced by the COM port you identified earlier and BlueSMiRF_Firmware_v1_0.bin is the firmware that you are updating to. Make sure to send an additional key to run the batch file.

batch_program.bat BlueSMiRF_Firmware_v1_0.bin COM4

batch_program.bat running esptool

After about 20 seconds, you should see the following message: Done programming! Ready for next board.

Successfully Programmed BlueSMiRF v2 - ESP32

The batch file runs the following commands, where COM4 is replaced with the COM port that the BlueSMiRF product enumerated at and BlueSMiRF_Firmware_vx_x.bin is the firmware you would like to load.

esptool.exe --chip esp32 --port COM4 --baud 921600 --before default_reset --after hard_reset write_flash -z --flash_mode dio --flash_freq 80m --flash_size 8MB 0x1000 bins/bootloader.bin 0x8000 bins/partitions.bin 0xe000 bins/boot_app0.bin 0x10000 BlueSMiRF_Firmware_v1_0.bin

Note

Some users have reported the 921600 baud rate does not work. Decrease this to 115200 as needed.

Tip

Finished programming the ESP32? Type Ctrl + C , Y , and Enter to exit the batch file. You can also close the window.

Upon completion, the BlueSMiRF v2 must be power cycled to exit bootloader mode. Once power cycled, the BlueSMiRF will start running the new firmware.

Note

We recommend disconnecting the USB cable from the USB-to-Serial Converter or your computer's COM port.

docs.title: macOS / Linux
docs.text:
Get esptool.py. Connect a USB A to C cable from your computer to the USB-to-Serial. Now identify the COM port the USB-to-serial device enumerated at.

If the COM port is not showing, be sure the unit is turned On. If an unknown device is appearing, you’ll need to install drivers for your USB-to-serial device (we'll assume that you are using the CH340).

Once the correct COM port is identified, head to the GitHub repo for the BlueSMiRF v2 binaries and download all the contents. Unzip the contents in a known directory and copy the path.

Download BlueSMiRF v2 Binaries GitHub Repo (ZIP)

Open a Terminal window and run the following command, where /dev/ttyUSB0 is replaced with the port that the USB-to-Serial board enumerated at and BlueSMiRF_Firmware_vx_x.bin is the firmware you would like to load.

py esptool.py --chip esp32 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud 921600 --before default_reset --after hard_reset write_flash -z --flash_mode dio --flash_freq 80m --flash_size 8MB 0x1000 bins/bootloader.bin 0x8000 bins/partitions.bin 0xe000 bins/boot_app0.bin 0x10000 BlueSMiRF_Firmware_vx_x.bin

Note

Some users have reported the 921600 baud rate does not work. Decrease this to 115200 as needed.

Tip

Finished programming the ESP32? Type Ctrl + C , Y , and Enter to exit the batch file. You can also close the window.

Upon completion, the BlueSMiRF must be power cycled to exit bootloader mode. Once power cycled, the BlueSMiRF will start running the new firmware.

Note

We recommend disconnecting the USB cable from the USB-to-Serial Converter or your computer's COM port.

docs.title: Pair Two BlueSMiRFs
docs.text:
In this example, we will connect two BlueSMiRF v2 boards to two separate serial ports. We will then send characters from one serial terminal to a second serial terminal.

The image below on the left shows the Serial Basic (CH340, USB-C) connected to the BlueSMiRF v2 Header using M/F jumper wires. Headers were used to easily remove and reconnect the BlueSMiRF v2 with headers. The image to the right shows the Serial Basic (CH340, micro-B) connected to the BlueSMiRF v2 PTH using M/F jumper wires. A row of female headers were soldered on the board. Extra long headers were placed between the female headers to easily remove and reconnect the BlueSMiRF v2 PTH as well.

USB-to-Serial Converter (CH340) to BlueSMiRF v2 Header with an Additional Stackable Header

USB-to-Serial Converter (CH340) to BlueSMiRF v2 PTH

Note

To distinguish between the two BlueSMiRFs, try labeling the two board. In this case, we chose had the one with male headers and the other one with female headers.

Connect the first BlueSMiRF v2 to your computer's COM port. In this case, it was COM13. Press and hold the PAIR button between 4 to 8 seconds. The Status and Connect LEDs will slowly blink back and forth. The Connect LED will begin to fade in and out after a few seconds. Open a serial terminal and connect to the first BlueSMiRF at 115200 baud.

First Serial Terminal

At this point, connect the second BlueSMiRF v2 to your computer's COM port. In this case, it was COM18. Press and hold the second BlueSMiRF's PAIR button between 4 to 8 seconds. The second BlueSMiRF will scan the area for another BlueSMiRF and connect. Once connected, the Connect LEDs on both boards will remain solid. Open a second serial terminal, and connect to the second BlueSMiRF at 115200 baud. Move both serial terminals side by side.

Second Serial Terminal

Start typing characters in the first serial terminal. You should see them in the second serial terminal!

Sending Characters through First Terminal

Receiving Characters through Second Terminal

Type a message in the second terminal window. You should see them in the first serial terminal!

Receiving Characters through First Serial Terminal

Sending Characters through Second Terminal

docs.title: Bluetooth Terminal
docs.text:
Note

Bluetooth classic (Serial Port Profile or SPP) is primarily supported. This Bluetooth protocol is supported on Android phones, most desktops, and laptops. The BlueSMiRF v2 also supports the BLE protocol, available on all Apple phones.

In this example, we will connect a BlueSMiRF v2 to a smartphone and send serial data using the Bluetooth classic protocol (also known as Serial Port Profile or SPP).

The image below shows the Serial Basic (CH340, USB-C) connected to the BlueSMiRF v2 Header using M/F jumper wires. Headers were used to easily remove and reconnect the BlueSMiRF v2 with headers.

BlueSMiRF v2 to SmartPhone Bluetooth Classic Serial Terminal with the RedBoard Plus

docs.title: Download the Serial Bluetooth Terminal App
docs.text:
Head to your smartphone's app store. In this case, we were on an Android smartphone and used Google Play Store to download the Serial Bluetooth Terminal app. This app is great for development, debugging, and general use when using the BlueSMiRF's SPP and BLE protocols.

Google Play: Serial Bluetooth Terminal

Note

If you have a different phone OS, there are many apps like the Serial Bluetooth Terminal available for different smartphones. Just do a search in your app store.

docs.title: Pair the BlueSMiRF v2 with your Smartphone
docs.text:
Once downloaded, turn on your Bluetooth and open your Bluetooth settings. Scroll down until you see the available devices. With BlueSMiRF powered up and in range, you should be able to see the device in discoverable mode listed as BlueSMiRF-ABCD, where ABCD is the last four hex digits of the Bluetooth MAC. In this case, it was BlueSMiRF-5A66.

BlueSMiRF Discovered on Android Smartphone

Click on the device to begin pairing. A message will pop up asking if you want to pair with the device. At this point, select Pair.

BlueSMiRF Discovered on Android Smartphone

Scroll up to your Paired devices and look for the BlueSMiRF to verify that it has paired with your phone.

BlueSMiRF-5A66 Showing Up as a Paired Bluetooth Device

docs.title: Sending Characters Between a BlueSMiRF and Smartphone
docs.text:
Open the Serial Bluetooth Terminal app.

Serial Bluetooth Terminal Opened

Click on the connect icon to the left of the trash can icon. If all is well, you will get a message indicating that the BlueSMiRF is connected.

Connected to BlueSMiRF-5A66

Open a serial terminal, and connect to the BlueSMiRF at 115200 baud. In this case, it was connected to COM13. Start typing characters in the serial terminal. You should see them in the Serial Bluetooth Terminal app!

Serial Terminal Connected to BlueSMiRF v2

Receiving Characters through the Serial Bluetooth Terminal

Connect a USB-to-Serial converter to the BlueSMiRF. Depending on the BlueSMiRF that you have, you may need to solder headers. Then connect the USB cable between the converter and your computer.

From the microcontroller, you will need to wire the following pins. Since the BlueSMiRF v2 includes logic level circuitry on the TX and RX pins, we can wire the SparkFun RedBoard Plus directly to the pin when the switch for the microcontroller's logic level is set to 5V. Users that want to also connect software serial RX pin can also wire the connection to the BlueSMiRF v2's TXO but it is not necessary. A 9V power supply and barrel jack adapter was used to power both boards. The + pin from the adapter was connected to the SerLCD's RAW pin which is regulated down to 3.3V. If you have not already, make sure to upload the Arduino example code from the basic serial UART example. Select the board (in this case, the Tools > Board > Arduino AVR Boards (arduino) > Arduino Uno) and COM port that the board enumerated to. Then hit the upload button.

/*
 OpenLCD is an LCD with serial/I2C/SPI interfaces.

 To get this code to work, attached an OpenLCD to an Arduino Uno using the following pins:
 RX (OpenLCD) to Pin 7 (Arduino)

#include <SoftwareSerial.h>

SoftwareSerial OpenLCD(6, 7); //RX, TX

byte counter = 0;

void setup()
{
  Serial.begin(9600); //Start serial communication at 9600 for debug statements
  Serial.println("OpenLCD Example Code");

  OpenLCD.begin(9600); //Start communication with OpenLCD
}

void loop()
{
  //Send the clear command to the display - this returns the cursor to the beginning of the display
  OpenLCD.write('|'); //Setting character
  OpenLCD.write('-'); //Clear display

  OpenLCD.print("Hello World!    Counter: "); //For 16x2 LCD
  //OpenLCD.print("Hello World!        Counter: "); //For 20x4 LCD
  OpenLCD.print(counter++);

  delay(250); //Hang out for a bit
}

docs.title: Firmware Overview
docs.text:
The BlueSMiRF v2 comes pre-programmed with the latest version of our open-source firmware. However, users are free to modify the firmware and/or reprogram their board for their purposes.

Our firmware provides short-range, point-to-point communication; allowing serial UART data to be transmitted between two Bluetooth devices. It includes support for both the SPP and BLE protocols and features a massive >10kB buffer for each RX and TX channel to compensate for transmission delays. The firmware also offers a set of AT-commands to configure the BlueSMiRF v2's settings: including the baud rate, flow control, LED mode, and Over-The-Air (OTA) updates over a 2.4GHz WiFi network to name a few.

  • Serial Bluetooth® Point-to-Point Communication
  • Bluetooth Protocols Supported
    • Serial Port Profile (SPP)
    • Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)
  • Firmware Over-the-Air (OTA) Updates via 2.4GHz WiFi

Bluetooth Protocols

While Bluetooth Classic (Serial Port Profile or "SPP") is the primary communication protocol, which makes it highly compatible with Android devices and most computers, the BlueSMiRF v2 also supports Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) protocol for connecting with Apple devices and other low-power devices.

docs.title: Manually Reprogramming
docs.text:
If for some reason the OTA method can't be used, users can also manually reprogram the microcontroller on the BlueSMiRF v2.

  1. Download the Firmware: Download and unzip the contents of the SparkFun_BlueSMiRF-v2_Binaries GitHub repository. Download BlueSMiRF v2 Binaries GitHub Repo (ZIP)

  2. Connect Hardware: Wire the BlueSMiRF v2 to a USB-to-Serial converter, ensuring the TX and RX connections are crossed over. To automatically trigger a reset, connect the converter's DTR pin to the BlueSMiRF v2's RST PTH pad. USB-to-Serial Converter BlueSMiRF v2 DTR RST (PTH Pad) RXI TXO RXI TXO 3V3 VCC GND GND

  3. Identify the Port: Find your USB-to-Serial COM port using Windows Device Manager or your macOS/Linux terminal (e.g., /dev/ttyUSB0).

    CH340 is on COM10 as shown in Device Manager

  4. Upload the Firmware: Open a command prompt or terminal, navigate to the unzipped firmware directory, and execute the appropriate flash command for your OS:

    • Windows: Run the following command in the command prompt 
      .\batch_program.bat .\<firmware_name.bin> <COM_PORT>
    • macOS/Linux: Run the following command in the terminal 
      ./batch_program.sh ./<firmware_name.bin> <COM_PORT>
    Script Details

    These scripts basically run the following command in a loop:

    <ESPTOOL_EXECUTABLE> --chip esp32 --port <COM_PORT> --baud 921600 --before default-reset --after hard-reset write-flash -z --flash-mode dio --flash-freq 80m --flash-size 8MB 0x1000 bins/bootloader.bin 0x8000 bins/partitions.bin 0xe000 bins/boot_app0.bin 0x10000 <BINARY_FILE>

    Where the the following are variables are replaced with:

    • Windows:
      • <ESPTOOL_EXECUTABLE>: esptool.exe
      • <COM_PORT>: COM# (i.e. COM4)
    • Linux/MacOS:
      • <ESPTOOL_EXECUTABLE>: esptool
      • <COM_PORT>: /dev/tty* (i.e. /dev/ttyUSB0)
    • <BINARY_FILE>: BlueSMiRF_Firmware_vx_x.bin

    Tip

    Some users have reported issues, where the 921600 baud rate does not work. If you encounter this problem, reduce the baud rate to 115200.

  5. Start the Programming Process: When prompted, press a keyboard key to start the programming process. batch_program.bat running esptool

  6. Enter Bootloader Mode: When the Connecting....... prompt pops up, press and hold the PAIR button.

    Tip

    Bootloader mode is active when the STATUS LED is dimly lit and the CONNECT LED is off.

  7. Wait for Process to Complete

  8. Reboot: Power cycle the BlueSMiRF by disconnecting and reconnecting power to exit bootloader mode and run the new firmware.

    Tip

    If you previously connected the DTR pin of the USB-to-Serial converter to the RST PTH pad on the BlueSMiRF v2, it isn't necessary to power cycle the board.

  9. Programming Complete:: Wait for the following prompt Done programming! Ready for next board.

    Successfully Programmed BlueSMiRF v2 - ESP32

  10. Next:

    • To exit, click Ctrl + C to exit the batch file. You can also just close the window.
    • Otherwise, connect another BlueSMiRF v2 to the USB-to-serial converter and click a keyboard key to program the next board

docs.title: ESP32 Pico-Mini
docs.text:
The brains of the BlueSMiRF v2 is an ESP32 Pico-Mini module. The Espressif series of ESP32 modules are a versatile, compact MCU modules with WiFi, BT, and BLE capabilities that target a wide variety of applications. At the core of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module is the ESP32-PICO-V3-02, a System-in-Package device, along with an integrated 8 MB SPI flash, 2 MB SPI PSRAM, and 40 MHz oscillator. While the ESP32 Pico-Mini module has twenty-seven multifunctional GPIO that are available, only seven of I/O pins are actually utilized on the BlueSMiRF v2.

The ESP32 PICO-MINI-02 module on the BlueSMiRF v2.

Note

The ESP32 module can get a little warm when operating; don't be alarmed, this is just heat dissipating from the internal components.

A thermal image of the BlueSMiRF v2.

General Features Pin Connections Firmware

Bootloader Mode

Users can manually force the ESP32 into the serial bootloader mode with the PAIR button, to upload new firmware to the BlueSMiRF v2. Please, refer to the PAIR Button section below for more information.

Programming the ESP32 in Arduino

To program the ESP32 Pico-Mini module in the Arduino IDE, users should select the ESP32 > ESP32 Dev Module from the Board Manager list. Users should also be aware that not all of the capabilities, listed above, are available in the Arduino IDE; the Espressif IDF should be utilized for the full capabilities of the ESP32. When programming the module with the Arduino IDE, only the following peripherals are supported:

  • Only two UART interfaces are available.
  • Only one SPI bus is defined.
  • Only one I2C bus is defined.

For more technical specifications on the I/O pins, you can refer to the schematics, ESP32 Pico-Mini module datasheet, ESP32 SoC datasheet, and documentation for the ESP32 Arduino core.

Digital PinsAnalog PinsPWM PinsDAC PinsSerial PinsSPI PinsI2C Pins

Any of the GPIO pins of the ESP32 module can function as digital pins. In the Arduino IDE, users will need to declare the pinMode() function for the pins used in this manner, in the setup of their sketch.

  • Input

    When configured properly, an input pin will be looking for a HIGH or LOW state. This functionality is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the digitalRead(pin) function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, digitalRead() returns a boolean value. Input pins are high impedance and takes very little current to move the input pin from one state to another.

  • Output

    When configured as an output the pin will be at a HIGH or LOW voltage. This functionality is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the digitalWrite(pin, value) function. Output pins are low impedance; this means that they can provide a relatively substantial amount of current to other circuits.

The ESP32 module provides a 12-bit ADC (Analog Digital Converters) input on eighteen of its I/O pins. This functionality is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the analogRead(pin) function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, analogRead() returns a 10-bit value. To change the resolution of the value returned by the analogRead() function, use the analogReadResolution(bits) function.

The ESP32 module supports up to sixteen channels of 20-bit PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) outputs on any of its I/O pins. This is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the analogWrite(pin, value) function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, analogWrite() accepts an 8-bit value. To change the resolution of the PWM signal for the analogWrite() function, use the analogWriteResolution(bits) function.

The ESP32 module supports up to two 8-bit DAC (Digital Analog Converters) outputs. This is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the dacWrite(pin, value); function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

DAC1 GPIO 25 DAC2 GPIO 26

The ESP32 module provides three UART ports. By default, the UART ports for Serial and Serial1 can be accessed through the Arduino IDE using the serial communication class. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

  • Serial UART Port

    RX0 GPIO 1 TX0 GPIO 3

  • Serial1 UART Port

    RX1 GPIO 21 TX1 GPIO 22

Tip

We have noticed that with the ESP32 Arduino core, Serial.available() does not operate instantaneously. This is due to an interrupt triggered by the UART, to empty the FIFO when the RX pin is inactive for two byte periods:

  • At 9600 baud, hwAvailable takes about 11 ms before the UART indicates that data was received from: ERROR .

    \[ (bytes + 2) * 1ms = 11ms \]

  • At 115200 baud, hwAvailable takes about 1 ms before the UART indicates that data was received from: ERROR .

    \[ (bytes + 2) * .087ms = 1ms \]

For more information, please refer to this chatroom discussion.

The ESP32 module provides three SPI buses. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the SPI class is configured to utilize pins GPIO 32 (SCK), GPIO 25 (POCI), GPIO 26 (PICO), and GPIO 27 (SS) for its chip select. In order to utilize the other SPI ports or objects, users will need to create a custom SPI object and declare which pins to access. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

SCK GPIO 32 (SCK) SDI or POCI GPIO 25 (MISO) SDO or PICO GPIO 26 (MOSI) CS* GPIO 27 (SS) Signal Nomenclature

To comply with the latest OSHW design practices, we have adopted the new SPI signal nomenclature (SDO/SDI and PICO/POCI). The terms Master and Slave are now referred to as Controller and Peripheral. The MOSI signal on a controller has been replaced with SDO or PICO. Please refer to this announcement on the decision to deprecate the MOSI/MISO terminology and transition to the SDO/SDI naming convention.

The ESP32 module module can support up to two I2C buses. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the Wire class is configured to utilize pins GPIO 20 (SDA) and GPIO 7 (SCL). In order to utilize another I2C port, users will need to create a custom Wire object and declare which pins to access. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

SCL0 GPIO 7 (SCL) SDA0 GPIO 20 (SDA)

    • SD card, SDIO, I2S, IR, pulse counter, TWAI/CAN, Ethernet MAC

With the pin multiplexing capabilities of the ESP32 SoC, various pins can have several functionalities. For more technical specifications on the I/O pins, please refer to the ESP32 SoC datasheet.

  • 18x 12-bit analog to digital converter (ADC) channels
  • 3x UARTs (only two are configured by default in the Arduino IDE, one UART is used for bootloading/debug)
  • 3x SPI (only one is configured by default in the Arduino IDE)
  • 2x I2C (only one is configured by default in the Arduino IDE)
  • 2x digital-to-analog converter (DAC) channels
  • 16x 20-bit PWM outputs
  • 10x Capacitive Touch Inputs

Warning

Users should be aware of the following nuances of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module:

  • All the GPIO are 3.3V pins.
    • The I/O pins are not 5V-tolerant! To interface with higher voltage components, a logic level adapter is recommended.
  • The ESP32 Pico-Mini is only compatible with 2.4GHz WiFi networks; it will not work on the 5GHz bands.
  • There are electrical limitations to the amount of current that the ESP32 Pico-Mini module can sink or source. For more details, check out the ESP32 Pico-Mini module datasheet.
  • There are some limitations to the ADC performance, see the Note from the ADC Characteristics section of the ESP32 SoC datasheet.
  • For details on the boot mode configuration, please refer to section 3.3 Strapping Pins of the ESP32 SoC datasheet.
Power Modes

The ESP32 Pico-Mini module has various power modes:

  • Active - The chip radio is powered on. The chip can receive, transmit, or listen.
  • Modem Sleep - The CPU is operational and the clock is configurable. The Wi-Fi/Bluetooth baseband and radio are disabled.
  • Light Sleep - The CPU is paused. The RTC memory and RTC peripherals, as well as the ULP coprocessor are running.
  • Deep Sleep - Only the RTC memory and RTC peripherals are powered on. The ULP coprocessor is functional.
  • Hibernation - Only one RTC timer on the slow clock and certain RTC GPIO active.
  • Off - Chip is powered off.

For more information on the power management of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module, pleaser refer to Section 4.4 and Tables: 8 and 9 of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module datasheet.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text:
The BlueSMiRF v2 comes pre-programmed with the latest version of our open-source firmware. However, users are free to modify the firmware and/or reprogram their board for their purposes.

Our firmware provides short-range, point-to-point communication; allowing serial UART data to be transmitted between two Bluetooth devices. It includes support for both the SPP and BLE protocols and features a massive >10kB buffer for each RX and TX channel to compensate for transmission delays. The firmware also offers a set of AT-commands to configure the BlueSMiRF v2's settings: including the baud rate, flow control, LED mode, and Over-The-Air (OTA) updates over a 2.4GHz WiFi network to name a few.

  • Serial Bluetooth® Point-to-Point Communication
  • Bluetooth Protocols Supported
    • Serial Port Profile (SPP)
    • Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)
  • Firmware Over-the-Air (OTA) Updates via 2.4GHz WiFi

Bluetooth Protocols

While Bluetooth Classic (Serial Port Profile or "SPP") is the primary communication protocol, which makes it highly compatible with Android devices and most computers, the BlueSMiRF v2 also supports Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) protocol for connecting with Apple devices and other low-power devices.

docs.text:
The BlueSMiRF v2 only requires 3.3V and is powered through the VCC and GND pins of its hardware connection.

The power pins from the BlueSMiRF v2's hardware connection.

Below, is a general summary of the power circuitry:

  • VCC - The input voltage for the BlueSMiRF v2, provided from its hardware connection
    • Supplies the AP2112 LDO regulator
      • Input Voltage Range: 3.3 to 6.0V (1)
      • Powers the ESP32 module, LEDs, and lower voltage of the logic-level shifters
      • The voltage regulator can be bypassed with the JP2 jumper
  • GND - The common ground or the 0V reference for the voltage supplies.
  1. While the input voltage range for the AP2112 LDO voltage regulator is 2.5 to 6.0V, we recommend a minimum input voltage of 3.3V to prevent the ESP32 module browning out.
Power Consumption

The board's power consumption is based on its operation. Here are some of estimates based on our measurements at 3.3V.

  • Connected with No Traffic: 75mA / 248mW
  • Connected with Duplex Traffic: 140mA / 462mW

docs.title: UART Interface
docs.text:
The UART interface provides access to the primary function of the BlueSMiRF v2. It supports full-duplex data transmission for baud rates ranging between 2400-921600bps.

The pins of the UART interface for the BlueSMiRF v2.

Device 1 RX TX CTS RTS Device 2 TX RX RTS CTS

The UART signals cross-coupled between two devices

Below, is a general summary of the UART interface:

  • Data Bus

    • Features logic-level converters; the higher voltage is supplied by VCC
    • Full-duplex support (simultaneous/bidirectional communication)
    • RXI - Data input to the BlueSMiRF v2 from its hardware connection
      • If connected, data received from the RXI pin is piped to its Bluetooth connection
      • Buffer Size: 51kB
    • TXO - Data output from the BlueSMiRF v2 to its hardware connection
      • If connected, data received from the Bluetooth connection is piped to its TXO pin
      • Buffer Size: 10kB

    Info

    By default, the baud rate is configured to 115200bps. Use the AT-SerialSpeed command to change this setting.

  • Flow Control (Optional)

    • Direct connection to GPIO; no logic-level conversion
    • Does not support legacy hardware flow control for DTE (Data Terminal Equipment) and DCE (Data Communications Equipment)
    • CTS - Connected device, controls data transmission from BlueSMiRF v2
      • HIGH: Connected device, signaling that it is ready for data to be sent
      • LOW: Connected device, signaling that the data transmission needs to be halted
    • RTS - Controls data transmission to the BlueSMiRF v2
      • HIGH: BlueSMiRF v2 is ready for data to be transmitted to it
      • LOW: BlueSMiRF v2 buffer is full; asserts LOW to halt data transmission

    Info

    By default, the flow control pins are disabled in the firmware. Use the AT-FlowControl=1 command to enable them.

    Tip

    The flow control pins aren't necessary for the BlueSMiRF v2 to function. However, when enabled, it assists with buffer control, device latency, and data synchronization.

Tip

These data bus and flow control signals need to be cross-coupled between the two devices.

docs.title: Pair Button
docs.text:
The PAIR button is used to switch between the various modes of operation for the BlueSMiRF v2. It is used to simplify pairing, triggering various modes of operation, and restoring the settings to their factory defaults.

PAIR Button on the BlueSMiRF v2.

  • Discoverable Mode
    • A default state, where the STATUS LED will fade in-and-out a few times to indicate the device is ready to be paired with a Bluetooth device.
  • BlueSMiRF Pairing Mode
    • Used to pair the BlueSMiRF v2 with another BlueSMiRF v2 in the (default) discoverable mode.
    • Press and hold the PAIR button down for 4 - 8sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth.
      • If the PAIR button is continued to be held, the device will transition to a factory reset (see below).
    • If the BlueSMiRF v2 hasn't been discovered or paired with the other BlueSMiRF v2 after a few seconds, it will return to the (default) discoverable mode and the STATUS LED will fade in-and-out a few times to indicate the transition.
  • Bootloader Mode
    • Used to manually update the firmware through the UART interface.
    • To enter bootloader mode, users will need to hold down the PAIR button while the BlueSMiRF v2 is not powered.
    • Continue holding down the PAIR button, while applying power to put the microcontroller into bootloader mode.
    • Release the button, to upload new firmware.
  • Factory Reset
    • Press and hold the PAIR button down for more than 8sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth, rapidly.
    • Once the user releases the button, the original factory settings are be applied and the BlueSMiRF v2 resets. Then, it returns to the (default) discoverable mode.

docs.title: LEDs
docs.text:
The BlueSMiRF v2 has two status LEDs, which function differently based on the Bluetooth connection and/or datastream status; in conjunction with the device's AT-LedStyle configuration setting and operation mode:

The status indication LEDs on the BlueSMiRF v2.

  • Normal Operation

    Setting: AT-LedStyle=0 (Default)
    • CONNECT - Indicates the Bluetooth connection status
      • Discoverable Mode: This LED will blink, while the BlueSMiRF v2 is available to be paired with.
      • Active Connection: This LED will turn solid, once the BlueSMiRF v2 has an active Bluetooth connection
    • STATUS - Indicates the status of the UART datastream
      • Data Transmission: The STATUS LED will blink, as data is sent to the BlueSMiRF v2.
    Setting: AT-LedStyle=1
    • CONNECT - Indicates the Bluetooth connection status and the status of the TXO datastream
      • Discoverable Mode: This LED will blink, regularly, while the BlueSMiRF v2 awaits for an active Bluetooth connection.
      • Active Connection
        • Initial Connection: Upon an initial connection, this LED will remain solid until data is passed through the TXO pin of the BlueSMiRF v2.
        • Data Transmission: This LED will blink as data is passed through the TXO pin of the BlueSMiRF v2.
    • STATUS - Indicates the status of the RXI datastream
      • Data Transmission: This LED will blink, as data is passed through the RXI pin of the BlueSMiRF v2; regardless of the Bluetooth connection status.

  • Pairing Mode

    • After the PAIR button has been held down for 4-8sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth.
      • If the PAIR button is continued to be held, the device will transition to a factory reset (see below).
    • After a few seconds in pairing mode, if the BlueSMiRF v2 hasn't been paired with, it will return to the (configured) discoverable mode and the STATUS LED will fade in-and-out a few times to indicate the transition.
  • Factory Reset
    • After the PAIR button has been held down past 8sec sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth, rapidly.
    • Once the user releases the button, the original factory settings are be applied and the BlueSMiRF v2 resets. Then, it returns to the (default) discoverable mode.
  • Command Mode
    • Upon entering command mode, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink simultaneously.

    • After an AT-command has been initially sent sent:

      Setting: AT-LedStyle=0 (Default)

      The LEDs will then return to functioning in the (default) normal operation.

      Setting: AT-LedStyle=1

      The LEDs will continue to blink simultaneously.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • Our BlueSMiRF product line is a series of wireless Bluetooth® serial links. The SparkFun BlueSMiRF v2 is a reboot of the previous BlueSMiRF board, utilizing the Espressif's ESP32 Pico Mini for wireless communication and comes in several variants, with PTH pads, male header pins, or a JST connector. These boards operate as a serial data link and are a great replacement for hardwired between boards. Simply connect a BlueSMiRF v2, pair the devices over Bluetooth®, and simultaneously transmit and receive data! Any serial stream from 2400 - 921600bps can be passed between two devices; with a range of 100' (33m). In this tutorial, we'll go over the hardware and the connections to a BlueSMiRF v2. We will also provide a few examples; including, how to connect to the BlueSMiRF v2 with a smartphone and a basic Arduino example transmitting data between two BlueSMiRF v2s... so let's get started!

docs.title: Create a Serial Link
docs.text:
1. Device 1: By default, the device be in discoverable mode and be available for pairing.
    • Device 1 will broadcast the name BlueSMiRF-Pairing and wait for an incoming connection.
  2. Device 2: Hold the PAIR button for 4 to 8 seconds, then release.
  3. Device 2: Will then enter pairing mode and scan for any compatible devices to pair with.
    • The scan should find that Device 1 is in discoverable mode broadcasting the BlueSMiRF-Pairing name.
  4. Device 2: Connects to Device 1
    • Device 2 stores the MAC address of Device 1
    • Whenever Device 2 boots up, it will always try to connect to the stored the MAC address (i.e. Device 1).
  5. Device 1: Remains agnostic of any connections or pairing; no MAC address has been stored on it.
    • When Device 1 boots, it will not attempt to connect to any devices.

Note

The BlueSMiRF that was detected (Device 1), does not store the MAC address of the pairing BlueSMiRF (Device 2). Upon restart, the BlueSMiRF (Device 1) will return to the (default) discoverable mode.

Back in April 2005, we released the original BlueSMiRF (Bluetooth Serial Miniature RF) Link, which featured BlueRadio's WML-C40AH Bluetooth modems. It was released in two variants that came with either a 4-pin header on the basic BlueSMiRF or a 6-pin header on the extended BlueSMiRF, using the following pin configuration (CTS)/PWR/GND/TX-O/RX-I/(RTS).

docs.title: Silver, Gold, and Mate
docs.text: Eventually, the Bluetooth modems manufactured by BlueRadio were discontinued and we transitioned to the RN-41 and RN-42 modules from Roving Network.

docs.title: Gold/Silver Variants
docs.text:
The primary difference between the RN-41 and RN-42 modules was their range/transmit power. The BlueSMiRF Gold featured the RN-41, a class 1 Bluetooth module that had a range of 100m, but utilized more power. Meanwhile, the BlueSMiRF Silver featured the RN-42, a class 2 module with lower power consumption and a range limited to 10m.

BlueSMiRF Gold (RN-41)

BlueSMiRF Silver (RN-42)

docs.title: Mate Header
docs.text:
With this revision, we also settled on a 6-pin layout to breakout the flow control pins of the serial interface. Additionally, in response to the growing popularity of miniaturized development boards, like the Arduino Pro and Pro Mini, we introduced a new variant with a compatible pin layout. The BlueSMiRF Mate variants had a pin layout ( GND/CTS/VCC/TXO/RXI/RTS) that matched the USB-to-Serial adapters that were used to program and interface with the development boards. This allowed users to easily extend the capabilities of their board with the BlueSMiRF Mate.

A comparison of the pin layouts between the Bluetooth Mate and regular BlueSMiRF

BlueSMiRF Mate connected to the headers for the serial programming interface of the Arduino Pro.

docs.title: The Next Generation (v2)
docs.text:
Just as the Bluetooth modems from BlueRadio were discontinued, production of the modules from Roving Network also ceased and in 2021 we sold the last of the BlueSMiRF Gold and Silver. Fast forward to January 2024 and the BlueSMiRF has arisen once more! The new BlueSMiRFs v2 features a few upgrades:

  • Features an ESP32-PICO-MINI-02 module programmed with our open-source firmware
    • Easily update the firmware Over-the-Air or through the serial interface
    • Remotely configure the settings with a simple AT-command set
  • We have three variants with different connections to simplify hooking up the BlueSMiRF to your project
    • The PTH pad and male header variants have fully, adopted the pin layout from the Bluetooth Mate
      • RTS/RXI/TXO/VCC/CTS/GND
      • Pin labels are now provided on both sides of the board
    • On the JST variant, the pin layout and JST connector matches the serial radios
  • A user button has been added to simplify pairing, triggering various modes of operation, and resetting the factory defaults
  • Upgraded the voltage regulator to the APA2112K 3.3V, 600mA for increased performance

docs.text: Eventually, the Bluetooth modems manufactured by BlueRadio were discontinued and we transitioned to the RN-41 and RN-42 modules from Roving Network.

docs.title: Gold/Silver Variants
docs.text:
The primary difference between the RN-41 and RN-42 modules was their range/transmit power. The BlueSMiRF Gold featured the RN-41, a class 1 Bluetooth module that had a range of 100m, but utilized more power. Meanwhile, the BlueSMiRF Silver featured the RN-42, a class 2 module with lower power consumption and a range limited to 10m.

docs.title: Mate Header
docs.text:
With this revision, we also settled on a 6-pin layout to breakout the flow control pins of the serial interface. Additionally, in response to the growing popularity of miniaturized development boards, like the Arduino Pro and Pro Mini, we introduced a new variant with a compatible pin layout. The BlueSMiRF Mate variants had a pin layout ( GND/CTS/VCC/TXO/RXI/RTS) that matched the USB-to-Serial adapters that were used to program and interface with the development boards. This allowed users to easily extend the capabilities of their board with the BlueSMiRF Mate.

A comparison of the pin layouts between the Bluetooth Mate and regular BlueSMiRF

docs.title: The Next Generation (v2)
docs.text:
Just as the Bluetooth modems from BlueRadio were discontinued, production of the modules from Roving Network also ceased and in 2021 we sold the last of the BlueSMiRF Gold and Silver. Fast forward to January 2024 and the BlueSMiRF has arisen once more! The new BlueSMiRFs v2 features a few upgrades:

  • Features an ESP32-PICO-MINI-02 module programmed with our open-source firmware
    • Easily update the firmware Over-the-Air or through the serial interface
    • Remotely configure the settings with a simple AT-command set
  • We have three variants with different connections to simplify hooking up the BlueSMiRF to your project
    • The PTH pad and male header variants have fully, adopted the pin layout from the Bluetooth Mate
      • RTS/RXI/TXO/VCC/CTS/GND
      • Pin labels are now provided on both sides of the board
    • On the JST variant, the pin layout and JST connector matches the serial radios
  • A user button has been added to simplify pairing, triggering various modes of operation, and resetting the factory defaults
  • Upgraded the voltage regulator to the APA2112K 3.3V, 600mA for increased performance

docs.title: ESP32 Pico-Mini
docs.text:
The brains of the BlueSMiRF v2 is an ESP32 Pico-Mini module. The Espressif series of ESP32 modules are a versatile, compact MCU modules with WiFi, BT, and BLE capabilities that target a wide variety of applications. At the core of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module is the ESP32-PICO-V3-02, a System-in-Package device, along with an integrated 8 MB SPI flash, 2 MB SPI PSRAM, and 40 MHz oscillator. While the ESP32 Pico-Mini module has twenty-seven multifunctional GPIO that are available, only seven of I/O pins are actually utilized on the BlueSMiRF v2.

The ESP32 PICO-MINI-02 module on the BlueSMiRF v2.

Note

The ESP32 module can get a little warm when operating; don't be alarmed, this is just heat dissipating from the internal components.

A thermal image of the BlueSMiRF v2.

General Features Pin Connections Firmware

Bootloader Mode

Users can manually force the ESP32 into the serial bootloader mode with the PAIR button, to upload new firmware to the BlueSMiRF v2. Please, refer to the PAIR Button section below for more information.

Programming the ESP32 in Arduino

To program the ESP32 Pico-Mini module in the Arduino IDE, users should select the ESP32 > ESP32 Dev Module from the Board Manager list. Users should also be aware that not all of the capabilities, listed above, are available in the Arduino IDE; the Espressif IDF should be utilized for the full capabilities of the ESP32. When programming the module with the Arduino IDE, only the following peripherals are supported:

  • Only two UART interfaces are available.
  • Only one SPI bus is defined.
  • Only one I2C bus is defined.

For more technical specifications on the I/O pins, you can refer to the schematics, ESP32 Pico-Mini module datasheet, ESP32 SoC datasheet, and documentation for the ESP32 Arduino core.

Digital PinsAnalog PinsPWM PinsDAC PinsSerial PinsSPI PinsI2C Pins

Any of the GPIO pins of the ESP32 module can function as digital pins. In the Arduino IDE, users will need to declare the pinMode() function for the pins used in this manner, in the setup of their sketch.

  • Input

    When configured properly, an input pin will be looking for a HIGH or LOW state. This functionality is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the digitalRead(pin) function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, digitalRead() returns a boolean value. Input pins are high impedance and takes very little current to move the input pin from one state to another.

  • Output

    When configured as an output the pin will be at a HIGH or LOW voltage. This functionality is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the digitalWrite(pin, value) function. Output pins are low impedance; this means that they can provide a relatively substantial amount of current to other circuits.

The ESP32 module provides a 12-bit ADC (Analog Digital Converters) input on eighteen of its I/O pins. This functionality is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the analogRead(pin) function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, analogRead() returns a 10-bit value. To change the resolution of the value returned by the analogRead() function, use the analogReadResolution(bits) function.

The ESP32 module supports up to sixteen channels of 20-bit PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) outputs on any of its I/O pins. This is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the analogWrite(pin, value) function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, analogWrite() accepts an 8-bit value. To change the resolution of the PWM signal for the analogWrite() function, use the analogWriteResolution(bits) function.

The ESP32 module supports up to two 8-bit DAC (Digital Analog Converters) outputs. This is accessed in the Arduino IDE using the dacWrite(pin, value); function. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

DAC1 GPIO 25 DAC2 GPIO 26

The ESP32 module provides three UART ports. By default, the UART ports for Serial and Serial1 can be accessed through the Arduino IDE using the serial communication class. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

  • Serial UART Port

    RX0 GPIO 1 TX0 GPIO 3

  • Serial1 UART Port

    RX1 GPIO 21 TX1 GPIO 22

Tip

We have noticed that with the ESP32 Arduino core, Serial.available() does not operate instantaneously. This is due to an interrupt triggered by the UART, to empty the FIFO when the RX pin is inactive for two byte periods:

  • At 9600 baud, hwAvailable takes about 11 ms before the UART indicates that data was received from: ERROR .

    \[ (bytes + 2) * 1ms = 11ms \]

  • At 115200 baud, hwAvailable takes about 1 ms before the UART indicates that data was received from: ERROR .

    \[ (bytes + 2) * .087ms = 1ms \]

For more information, please refer to this chatroom discussion.

The ESP32 module provides three SPI buses. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the SPI class is configured to utilize pins GPIO 32 (SCK), GPIO 25 (POCI), GPIO 26 (PICO), and GPIO 27 (SS) for its chip select. In order to utilize the other SPI ports or objects, users will need to create a custom SPI object and declare which pins to access. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

SCK GPIO 32 (SCK) SDI or POCI GPIO 25 (MISO) SDO or PICO GPIO 26 (MOSI) CS* GPIO 27 (SS) Signal Nomenclature

To comply with the latest OSHW design practices, we have adopted the new SPI signal nomenclature (SDO/SDI and PICO/POCI). The terms Master and Slave are now referred to as Controller and Peripheral. The MOSI signal on a controller has been replaced with SDO or PICO. Please refer to this announcement on the decision to deprecate the MOSI/MISO terminology and transition to the SDO/SDI naming convention.

The ESP32 module module can support up to two I2C buses. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the Wire class is configured to utilize pins GPIO 20 (SDA) and GPIO 7 (SCL). In order to utilize another I2C port, users will need to create a custom Wire object and declare which pins to access. By default, in the Arduino IDE, the ESP32 Dev Module board definition supports:

SCL0 GPIO 7 (SCL) SDA0 GPIO 20 (SDA)

docs.text:
• Electrical Characteristics:

  • Xtensa® Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 Microprocessor (up to 240MHz)

    • Frequency Range: 2412 - 2484MHz

      • BR/EDR

    • Transmitter Class: 1, 2, and 3
  • 27 GPIO (including strapping pins)
  • Other Supported Peripherals:
    • SD card, SDIO, I2S, IR, pulse counter, TWAI/CAN, Ethernet MAC

With the pin multiplexing capabilities of the ESP32 SoC, various pins can have several functionalities. For more technical specifications on the I/O pins, please refer to the ESP32 SoC datasheet.

  • 18x 12-bit analog to digital converter (ADC) channels
  • 3x UARTs (only two are configured by default in the Arduino IDE, one UART is used for bootloading/debug)
  • 3x SPI (only one is configured by default in the Arduino IDE)
  • 2x I2C (only one is configured by default in the Arduino IDE)
  • 2x digital-to-analog converter (DAC) channels
  • 16x 20-bit PWM outputs
  • 10x Capacitive Touch Inputs

Warning

Users should be aware of the following nuances of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module:

  • All the GPIO are 3.3V pins.
    • The I/O pins are not 5V-tolerant! To interface with higher voltage components, a logic level adapter is recommended.
  • The ESP32 Pico-Mini is only compatible with 2.4GHz WiFi networks; it will not work on the 5GHz bands.
  • There are electrical limitations to the amount of current that the ESP32 Pico-Mini module can sink or source. For more details, check out the ESP32 Pico-Mini module datasheet.
  • There are some limitations to the ADC performance, see the Note from the ADC Characteristics section of the ESP32 SoC datasheet.
  • For details on the boot mode configuration, please refer to section 3.3 Strapping Pins of the ESP32 SoC datasheet.
Power Modes

The ESP32 Pico-Mini module has various power modes:

  • Active - The chip radio is powered on. The chip can receive, transmit, or listen.
  • Modem Sleep - The CPU is operational and the clock is configurable. The Wi-Fi/Bluetooth baseband and radio are disabled.
  • Light Sleep - The CPU is paused. The RTC memory and RTC peripherals, as well as the ULP coprocessor are running.
  • Deep Sleep - Only the RTC memory and RTC peripherals are powered on. The ULP coprocessor is functional.
  • Hibernation - Only one RTC timer on the slow clock and certain RTC GPIO active.
  • Off - Chip is powered off.

For more information on the power management of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module, pleaser refer to Section 4.4 and Tables: 8 and 9 of the ESP32 Pico-Mini module datasheet.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text:
The BlueSMiRF v2 comes pre-programmed with the latest version of our open-source firmware. However, users are free to modify the firmware and/or reprogram their board for their purposes.

Our firmware provides short-range, point-to-point communication; allowing serial UART data to be transmitted between two Bluetooth devices. It includes support for both the SPP and BLE protocols and features a massive >10kB buffer for each RX and TX channel to compensate for transmission delays. The firmware also offers a set of AT-commands to configure the BlueSMiRF v2's settings: including the baud rate, flow control, LED mode, and Over-The-Air (OTA) updates over a 2.4GHz WiFi network to name a few.

  • Serial Bluetooth® Point-to-Point Communication
  • Bluetooth Protocols Supported
    • Serial Port Profile (SPP)
    • Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)
  • Firmware Over-the-Air (OTA) Updates via 2.4GHz WiFi

Bluetooth Protocols

While Bluetooth Classic (Serial Port Profile or "SPP") is the primary communication protocol, which makes it highly compatible with Android devices and most computers, the BlueSMiRF v2 also supports Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) protocol for connecting with Apple devices and other low-power devices.

The BlueSMiRF v2 only requires 3.3V and is powered through the VCC and GND pins of its hardware connection.

The power pins from the BlueSMiRF v2's hardware connection.

Below, is a general summary of the power circuitry:

  • VCC - The input voltage for the BlueSMiRF v2, provided from its hardware connection

      • Input Voltage Range: 3.3 to 6.0V (1)

Power Consumption

  • Connected with No Traffic: 75mA / 248mW

docs.title: UART Interface
docs.text:
The UART interface provides access to the primary function of the BlueSMiRF v2. It supports full-duplex data transmission for baud rates ranging between 2400-921600bps.

The pins of the UART interface for the BlueSMiRF v2.

Device 1 RX TX CTS RTS Device 2 TX RX RTS CTS

The UART signals cross-coupled between two devices

Below, is a general summary of the UART interface:

  • Data Bus

    • Features logic-level converters; the higher voltage is supplied by VCC
    • Full-duplex support (simultaneous/bidirectional communication)
    • RXI - Data input to the BlueSMiRF v2 from its hardware connection
      • If connected, data received from the RXI pin is piped to its Bluetooth connection
      • Buffer Size: 51kB
    • TXO - Data output from the BlueSMiRF v2 to its hardware connection
      • If connected, data received from the Bluetooth connection is piped to its TXO pin
      • Buffer Size: 10kB

    Info

    By default, the baud rate is configured to 115200bps. Use the AT-SerialSpeed command to change this setting.

  • Flow Control (Optional)

    • Direct connection to GPIO; no logic-level conversion
    • Does not support legacy hardware flow control for DTE (Data Terminal Equipment) and DCE (Data Communications Equipment)
    • CTS - Connected device, controls data transmission from BlueSMiRF v2
      • HIGH: Connected device, signaling that it is ready for data to be sent
      • LOW: Connected device, signaling that the data transmission needs to be halted
    • RTS - Controls data transmission to the BlueSMiRF v2
      • HIGH: BlueSMiRF v2 is ready for data to be transmitted to it
      • LOW: BlueSMiRF v2 buffer is full; asserts LOW to halt data transmission

    Info

    By default, the flow control pins are disabled in the firmware. Use the AT-FlowControl=1 command to enable them.

    Tip

    The flow control pins aren't necessary for the BlueSMiRF v2 to function. However, when enabled, it assists with buffer control, device latency, and data synchronization.

Tip

These data bus and flow control signals need to be cross-coupled between the two devices.

docs.title: Pair Button
docs.text:
The PAIR button is used to switch between the various modes of operation for the BlueSMiRF v2. It is used to simplify pairing, triggering various modes of operation, and restoring the settings to their factory defaults.

PAIR Button on the BlueSMiRF v2.

  • Discoverable Mode
    • A default state, where the STATUS LED will fade in-and-out a few times to indicate the device is ready to be paired with a Bluetooth device.
  • BlueSMiRF Pairing Mode
    • Used to pair the BlueSMiRF v2 with another BlueSMiRF v2 in the (default) discoverable mode.
    • Press and hold the PAIR button down for 4 - 8sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth.
      • If the PAIR button is continued to be held, the device will transition to a factory reset (see below).
    • If the BlueSMiRF v2 hasn't been discovered or paired with the other BlueSMiRF v2 after a few seconds, it will return to the (default) discoverable mode and the STATUS LED will fade in-and-out a few times to indicate the transition.
  • Bootloader Mode
    • Used to manually update the firmware through the UART interface.
    • To enter bootloader mode, users will need to hold down the PAIR button while the BlueSMiRF v2 is not powered.
    • Continue holding down the PAIR button, while applying power to put the microcontroller into bootloader mode.
    • Release the button, to upload new firmware.
  • Factory Reset
    • Press and hold the PAIR button down for more than 8sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth, rapidly.
    • Once the user releases the button, the original factory settings are be applied and the BlueSMiRF v2 resets. Then, it returns to the (default) discoverable mode.

docs.title: LEDs
docs.text:
The BlueSMiRF v2 has two status LEDs, which function differently based on the Bluetooth connection and/or datastream status; in conjunction with the device's AT-LedStyle configuration setting and operation mode:

The status indication LEDs on the BlueSMiRF v2.

  • Normal Operation

    Setting: AT-LedStyle=0 (Default)
    • CONNECT - Indicates the Bluetooth connection status
      • Discoverable Mode: This LED will blink, while the BlueSMiRF v2 is available to be paired with.
      • Active Connection: This LED will turn solid, once the BlueSMiRF v2 has an active Bluetooth connection
    • STATUS - Indicates the status of the UART datastream
      • Data Transmission: The STATUS LED will blink, as data is sent to the BlueSMiRF v2.
    Setting: AT-LedStyle=1
    • CONNECT - Indicates the Bluetooth connection status and the status of the TXO datastream
      • Discoverable Mode: This LED will blink, regularly, while the BlueSMiRF v2 awaits for an active Bluetooth connection.
      • Active Connection
        • Initial Connection: Upon an initial connection, this LED will remain solid until data is passed through the TXO pin of the BlueSMiRF v2.
        • Data Transmission: This LED will blink as data is passed through the TXO pin of the BlueSMiRF v2.
    • STATUS - Indicates the status of the RXI datastream
      • Data Transmission: This LED will blink, as data is passed through the RXI pin of the BlueSMiRF v2; regardless of the Bluetooth connection status.

  • Pairing Mode

    • After the PAIR button has been held down for 4-8sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth.
      • If the PAIR button is continued to be held, the device will transition to a factory reset (see below).
    • After a few seconds in pairing mode, if the BlueSMiRF v2 hasn't been paired with, it will return to the (configured) discoverable mode and the STATUS LED will fade in-and-out a few times to indicate the transition.
  • Factory Reset
    • After the PAIR button has been held down past 8sec sec, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink back-and-forth, rapidly.
    • Once the user releases the button, the original factory settings are be applied and the BlueSMiRF v2 resets. Then, it returns to the (default) discoverable mode.
  • Command Mode
    • Upon entering command mode, the CONNECT and STATUS LED will blink simultaneously.

    • After an AT-command has been initially sent sent:

      Setting: AT-LedStyle=0 (Default)

      The LEDs will then return to functioning in the (default) normal operation.

      Setting: AT-LedStyle=1

      The LEDs will continue to blink simultaneously.
